Inference: an alert with no cheap follow-up fails both tests.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a line of 80 to 100 G with a one-minute baseline-comparison test, so that "you know immediately whether or not they can go back in" (npgdKKdJSww [09:36]). He says this does not exist yet.

---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: sports-analytics-and-decision-making
book: ssac-talks--42analytics
chapter: "npgdKKdJSww"
topic: cost of perfect detection
category: [concussion, availability, back-of-envelope-model]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-10-01
source: "npgdKKdJSww, SSAC12, 2012 SSAC - EOS Concussion Technology.m4v"
---

# If every concussion were caught and managed strictly, about one in five players would be out at any time

**What it is** — A back-of-envelope availability model. The speaker, using the survey figure that about half of athletes have a concussion each year, takes a 50-person football team with half concussed (25 players) and 10 days out each: 250 days, "about 4% of playing days", "not completely disruptive" (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]). He then argues recovery is longer than 10 days (see the vulnerability-window entry) and reruns it at 60 days out: "21% of playing days", "one out of five athletes out at all times", about four of a football team's starters and one hockey starter at any moment, not counting repeat concussions (npgdKKdJSww [13:43], [14:14]). His conclusion is that either medical guidelines get much looser ("which won't happen") or the games change, starting with how much contact they contain (npgdKKdJSww [14:45], [22:58]).

He says he did the math "on the plane" and that "the science is iffy" on the 10-day figure (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]).

**Why it works** — It is arithmetic on three assumed inputs: incidence, days out, and playing days in a season. The speaker gives the first two and not the third. Inference: 250 days equal 4% only if the team has about 6,250 player-days (50 players over about 125 days), and the 60-day case then gives 1,500 days over 6,250, or 24%, not the 21% he states; the two figures are not exactly proportional and the denominator is not shown. Treat both as rough.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to test a proposed detection or return-to-play standard against roster availability before adopting it: ask what the standard would cost in player-days if applied to every case.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's role in return to performance is to supply information that supports Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance decisions (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and it "doesn't assess readiness" in return to play, because "the template answers that" (interview 2026-09-28, Q22, Explicit). Inference: an availability estimate like this one is the kind of information Applied Performance could supply; the clearance standard itself stays with Athletic Medicine.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use the 4% or 21% figures as estimates for Baylor or for any real team. The 50% incidence is a survey figure from the speaker's other studies; the 10-day and 60-day recoveries are assumptions, and the 60-day case is the speaker's hypothetical of what very sensitive tests might demand, not a clinical standard. The model ignores repeat concussions, position differences and substitutions. It is a 2012 talk, and the speaker discloses a consultant role and a test-owner tie (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a 50-person football team, 25 concussed, 60 days out each, "four guys out on your football team every week out of your starting group" (npgdKKdJSww [14:14]).

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]] (source of the 50% input); [[claim--concussion-vulnerability-window-longer-than-return-rules-assumed]] (source of the 30 to 60 day input); [[claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football]] (the lever the speaker proposes in response).

type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: sports-analytics-and-decision-making
book: ssac-talks--42analytics
chapter: "npgdKKdJSww"
topic: hit count exposure budget
category: [concussion, exposure-monitoring, load-management]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-10-01
source: "npgdKKdJSww, SSAC12, 2012 SSAC - EOS Concussion Technology.m4v"
---

# A "hit count" for head impacts, modeled on baseball's pitch count

**What it is** — The speaker proposes counting head impacts the way baseball counts pitches: a cumulative exposure with a limit and rest, because subconcussive blows (hits that cause no clinical symptoms and pass the usual tests) may still injure the brain (npgdKKdJSww [15:46], [16:16]). He says the NFL let him announce the goal of a hit count at a Super Bowl press conference (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). The steps he gives:
- Model it on the pitch count: age caps (75 pitches at age 10, 85 at 11) plus mandatory rest (three days after 61 pitches). He admits those numbers are "clearly not based on much science" ("every number ends on five"), and accepts that as good enough to protect people (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]).
- Accept that low-level bumps are probably harmless, that damage is probable from some level up to concussive levels, and that the middle is unknown; lowering the number of hits lowers concussion risk too (npgdKKdJSww [17:50]).
- Count with sensors: he says college football players take "somewhere between 500 and 1,000 blows", one high school player took 2,235 blows above 10 G in 3 months, hockey players average a few hundred, and some near a thousand (npgdKKdJSww [18:20]).
- Pick a line, knowing "no one knows what that is" (npgdKKdJSww [18:20], [18:51]).
- Look by position: average force is about the same across football positions but totals differ: wide receivers under 400, linemen near or well over 1,000. An arbitrary cap of 500 would leave linemen, running backs and linebackers unable to finish a season (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]).

He also adds exposure across sports: 2,000 in football, about 1,000 in ice hockey, a couple of thousand in soccer, "probably no child" should take 5,000 head hits a year (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]), and a soccer-heading study (caption "Lipton", unpublished, diffusion tensor imaging) in which players taking up to 5,000 headers a year with over 1,300 were more likely to have cognitive and imaging abnormalities in their early 30s (npgdKKdJSww [20:55]).

**Why it works** — His analogy is that "your elbow will wear out" with too many throws and "your brain will wear out" with too many hits, with the brain more important (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). He gives no dose-response data for the brain. Inference: the idea works as a monitoring structure (count, cap, rest) even before a safe number is known, because it makes exposure visible by position and by week.

**When to apply** — When building an exposure report by position group, where counts per athlete are the output and a cap is not yet set. Inference: a weekly count by position, shown to Athletic Medicine and the coaching staff, is the decision aid; a cap needs Baylor's own data over several seasons.

Eric's baseline: abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver and progressions are kept smooth (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); there is no formal injury-risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12), and ACWR is looked at but not trusted ("raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context"). The course material also warns that heavy load-monitoring culture can push teams toward under-preparing athletes (Inferred, transcript, course team position); the speaker gives no evidence on that trade-off.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not set a cap from any number in the talk: the speaker says no one knows the line, the 5,000-header study is unpublished and from soccer, and the sensor counts are a few cases in football and hockey with no validity data for the devices. The talk's youth examples (Pop Warner, a high school player) do not give college thresholds. Impact sensors in 2012 recorded linear acceleration only, and the speaker says some marketing was "unethical" (npgdKKdJSww [08:04]). Using GPS-unit collision output as a head-impact proxy is an inference this talk does not support.

**Example** — The speaker's own positional comparison: receivers under 400 impacts, linemen near or over 1,000 at about the same average force (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]). The caption at [18:51] ("th000") is garbled; the figure is as read.

**Related** — [[framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing]]; [[claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football]]; [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]] (the baseball pitch-count program this one is modeled on, from a 2017 talk); [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (the exposure evidence behind pitch counts, from a 2015 talk).

# Cutting contact in practice is the main lever on head-impact exposure

**What it is** — The speaker's stated focus is "reducing hitting in practice", the "number one way" to restrict total counts, because in football "up to 75%" of brain trauma exposure happens in practice (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]). He gives three policy moves as evidence that people are "buying in":
- In the NFL collective bargaining talks the players' union pushed for 14 practice days with contact in 18 weeks (npgdKKdJSww [19:23]).

# The post-concussion "window of vulnerability" is longer than return-to-play practice assumed

**What it is** — The speaker defines the window of vulnerability as the period after a concussion in which further physical or cognitive trauma is "much more damaging", slower to recover from and may lead to permanent deficits; his comparison is to playing on a broken leg (npgdKKdJSww [04:04], [04:34]). He says the window is "dramatically" longer than believed:
- In 2008 athletes were still being sent back within 15 minutes if symptoms cleared on the sideline (npgdKKdJSww [12:43]).
- The window in rats is 7 to 10 days (npgdKKdJSww [12:43], [13:13]).
- Research tests (magnetic resonance spectroscopy, fMRI, blood flow, evoked potentials) find that "no one seems to recover to baseline" on the hardest tests within 30 days, so "their brain is abnormal" (npgdKKdJSww [13:13], [13:43]).
- The working rule he describes is that an athlete abnormal against his baseline neuropsychological test cannot go back in (npgdKKdJSww [13:43]).

He cites a recent case (a pro hockey star still out; a basketball star back in three days) as a failure to respect the window (npgdKKdJSww [04:34], [05:04]). His caution on his own claim: "I'm with a short time... so don't criticize the science" (npgdKKdJSww [13:13]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that a concussion "starts a Cascade of events" that leaves the brain vulnerable (npgdKKdJSww [04:34]); he does not describe the cascade. Inference: the rat figure and the abnormal research scans are indirect evidence for a human clinical window, and the speaker moves from them to a longer clinical window without showing the link.

**When to apply** — As a reason to be wary of any return-to-play criterion built on clinical symptom clearance alone, and when a stakeholder asks why concussion return takes longer than other injuries. It is context for Athletic Medicine's process, not a rule for Applied Performance testing.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance does not assess readiness in return to play: "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q22). The baseline holds no concussion criteria and no recovery-window rules.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use "no one recovers within 30 days" as a clinical return criterion: abnormal research imaging is not the same as unreadiness, and the speaker admits to broad strokes and to the 60-day figure being a hypothetical (npgdKKdJSww [13:43]). The rat window is animal data, with no human study shown. The speaker's "15 minutes in 2008" is a statement of past practice, not a cited study. The talk is from 2012; consensus guidance has changed, so check current guidelines with Athletic Medicine. Return-to-play decisions on concussion are medical decisions.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a basketball star "back in three days" after a concussion, described as "ridiculous" (npgdKKdJSww [05:04]); the speaker's view, not a measured case.

**Related** — [[claim--diagnosed-concussion-rates-undercount-survey-and-observer-rates]]; [[claim--perfect-concussion-detection-would-sideline-one-fifth-of-players]] (the availability cost of taking this window seriously); [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] (Harries: a different view of what return criteria must include, for non-concussion injuries).

# After UCL ("Tommy John") surgery, about 80% return, but whether performance rises is disputed

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig (title spelling; caption "fleig") of the American Sports Medicine Institute (ASMI) reviews what happens to pitchers after ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (AgouMNTeyo4 [06:08]).

Return and time:
- Three studies in the same journal, on largely the same pitchers, tracked how pitchers did afterward: one covering 1974 to 2012, one of 147 pitchers since 1999, one of the 38 most recent pitchers with PitchFX data since 2008 (caption names "Ericson", "mcne", "Jang"; spellings unverified) (AgouMNTeyo4 [20:04], [20:35], [21:05]).
- About 80% of major leaguers return, 20% do not; in the middle study 80% made it back for at least one game but only about 67% "made it back and stayed there" (AgouMNTeyo4 [22:10], [22:40]).
- Published studies put the return to the majors at about a year and a half; ASMI's own data (Dr Andrews' patients, major league, minor league or amateur) show about 80% return in about 12 months, and he explains the gap as waiting for the next season (AgouMNTeyo4 [22:40], [24:15]).
- Age at surgery does not change the roughly 80% chance of returning to the same level or higher (high school, college, pro), but for a 16 year old "we don't have enough long-term data" and he calls it "a worrisome road" (AgouMNTeyo4 [56:34], [57:05]).

Performance: the first study said pitchers got better after surgery; the other two did not, finding performance "down like controls", that is, as an age-matched decline would predict. Fleisig says "I kind of believe" the second and third (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:05], [21:39], [22:10]). He adds that his own group's pitchers' stats "went down like the controls" (AgouMNTeyo4 [23:43]).

Definitions of success: the cited studies used at least 10 major league games; Fleisig says he would define success as staying healthy (off the disabled list, no repeat surgery) and statistics that match the age group (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:32], [54:02], [54:32]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig's explanation for the performance disagreement is age: pitchers having surgery at 30 or 33 would naturally decline, so comparing to the pre-surgery self overstates the change (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:39]). Inference: the three studies differ in who is counted and in what the comparator is, which is why a trajectory matched to age or role is the better yardstick.

**When to apply** — When defining what "back" means for an athlete returning from a major surgery: define it by several criteria, set the comparison to an age- and role-expected path, and state the time window before anyone judges the return.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports return-to-performance decisions with information (Explicit, Playbook p.6), contributes "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions, and the involvement "doesn't really end" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4, Q4a). A written protocol exists in the UE and LE rehab templates, but Flint has not read them. Inference: Fleisig's multi-part success definition could be set against those templates once staged; the baseline does not hold return criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — Elbow reconstruction in baseball pitchers only; do not transfer the 80%, 67% or 12 to 18 month figures to football or to other injuries. The 16% prevalence and 25% major league figures and the ASMI return data come from a study he says is unpublished or from his own center (AgouMNTeyo4 [08:13], [23:11]). The three-study summary has garbled author names, and the speaker says he is not a medical doctor (AgouMNTeyo4 [19:33]). The studies disagree with each other and with a later talk's claim that research shows no performance gain; the 2017 speaker also reports that, preliminarily, players with a second surgery came back less strongly (sHXuxj3-rbQ [04:12]). The "10 games" definition is a low bar for a star.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the question from the audience about two high-profile pitchers returning, where he said one game back "is not enough" and "marginal major leaguers" can pass a 10-game bar (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:32], [54:02]).

**Related** — [[claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents]] (what players expect the surgery to do, from a 2017 talk that cites a survey also shown here at [18:30]); [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]]; [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] (Harries).

# Youth pitchers with over 100 competitive innings in a year had more than three times the serious-injury risk

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig reports a prospective cohort from his center (ASMI): about 500 youth pitchers were called every week during a season to ask how much they pitched and whether the elbow or shoulder hurt, then called once a year for 10 years, "started out as little kids" and ended as about 22 year olds or out of the game (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:28]). Result: pitchers who pitched more than 100 innings in competition in any year of the study were "more than three times" as likely to have a serious elbow or shoulder injury needing surgery or making them quit baseball (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:58]). His one-line takeaway from all his data: "too much pitching leads to injury" (AgouMNTeyo4 [34:02]). Throwing is natural, but "excessive pitching is not natural": 100 full-effort pitches every fifth day is not (AgouMNTeyo4 [34:32]).

The 2017 league-office speaker cites a ten-year youth study with the same finding, 100 or more innings in a year, and does not name it (sHXuxj3-rbQ [07:54]); the two talks probably refer to the same work, which neither confirms.

**When to apply** — As the evidence base for any exposure cap on overhead throwing in youth baseball, and as the model for how to get exposure evidence: a defined cohort, short-interval exposure logging, long follow-up.

Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load and density in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). No formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this is cohort evidence for a dose, which is a different thing from an ACWR model Eric does not trust.

**When NOT to apply** — Youth baseball pitchers only; the speaker is explicit that these are kids who "started out as little kids". Do not set a college or professional innings limit from 100. The talk gives no confidence interval, adjustment for confounders or counts of injuries, so the "more than three times" is as stated, not a fitted estimate. Fleisig reports his own center's study and advises Little League, MLB, USA Baseball and a device company (AgouMNTeyo4 [06:08], [41:13]). Do not transfer to football or to Baylor athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own cohort result above (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:58]).

# Pitchers who often pitch while fatigued carry the largest odds of having had elbow surgery

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig compares pitchers who came to his center for surgery with pitchers who never had surgery, asking about their backgrounds (AgouMNTeyo4 [31:58], [32:30]). He frames the answers as bets: someone who often threw more than 80 pitches in a game: "4 to 1" that he has the scar; someone who pitched more than 8 months a year: "5 to 1" (the "8 months" is caption-dependent); someone who often pitched when fatigued: "36 to 1" (the caption reads "$36 to $1" and "3600%") (AgouMNTeyo4 [32:30], [33:00], [33:31]). He calls the fatigue result "the biggest result I found" in all his studies and says "you could throw everything else away" and keep it: pitchers who keep pitching after they are fatigued end up with serious injury (AgouMNTeyo4 [33:31]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig gives no mechanism. Inference: fatigue is a state in which each additional pitch is thrown with less control, which would plausibly add stress; the speaker does not say this, and he measured history, not mechanics, in this comparison.

**When to apply** — When the question is which exposure is the most modifiable for a throwing athlete's history: fatigue behavior (continuing when tired) and volume (pitches per game, months per year). Pair with the prospective 100-innings result rather than using the odds alone.

Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye is treated as at least as important as technology for daily assessment (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed); the eye flags where to look and data then investigates ("There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further," interview 2026-09-28, Q6, Explicit). Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes gamed them, and are kept for return to play and chronic conditions (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: the speaker's "fatigued" is a history item the athlete reports; Eric's survey experience is a reason to doubt a self-reported fatigue score used daily.

**When NOT to apply** — These are retrospective odds from recalled history, not a prospective rate: there is no control for who tells the story, for when pitchers were asked, or for who came in for surgery in the first place. The speaker states the odds as spoken wagers and gives no sample size, no confidence interval and no definition of "often" or "fatigued". He says in his Q&A that fatigue cannot be measured scientifically in the moment. The caption wording of the three odds ("8 months", "$36 to $1") is uncertain. Do not treat 36 to 1 as an individual risk score or transfer it to football. The speaker advises MLB, Little League, USA Baseball and a device company.

**Example** — The speaker's own: "if I ask you have you often pitched when you're fatigued... I'll bet you 36 to 1 that he's in the group that has had surgery" (paraphrased from AgouMNTeyo4 [32:30] to [33:31], the caption is garbled).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]]; [[heuristic--fatigue-is-individual-read-it-next-day-with-trainer-knowledge]] (his Q&A answer on how to see fatigue); [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] (Old Bull).

# A failed attempt to prove that curveballs are more dangerous than fastballs

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig says ASMI had advised for years not to throw curveballs until the growth plates close ("don't throw curve balls until you're old enough to shave") and ran studies to prove it (AgouMNTeyo4 [38:40], [39:11]). The result went the other way:
- Lab: in three biomechanics studies (two in Birmingham, one in Connecticut, some by other groups), elbow torque in a curveball was the same as or a little less than in a fastball (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [39:41]).
- Field: in the 10-year cohort of about 500 youth pitchers, those who started throwing curveballs younger were not the ones who got hurt (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12]).
- Conclusion: "we have not proven that the curve ball is dangerous. We have proven pitching too much is dangerous" (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12], [40:42]).

In Q&A he is careful: failing to prove danger is not proving safety, so young pitchers should still learn a fastball and a changeup first and add a curveball "when you're ready", because the purpose of off-speed pitches is to disturb the batter's timing (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31], [53:02]). On pitch type, his group has studied fastballs, curveballs, changeups and sliders: fastballs, curveballs and sliders are stressful, changeups less so; split-fingered fastballs were not studied (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:02]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig's measure of stress is elbow torque calculated from motion capture: kinematics (positions and angles) from cameras and kinetics (forces) calculated by equation, torque of about 100 N·m at the cocked position for a fastball (AgouMNTeyo4 [11:46], [12:17], [15:27]). Inference: if torque is the right proxy for ligament load, a pitch with equal torque should carry equal ligament risk; the speaker does not test that proxy in this talk (he says the link from arm stress to injury is unproven, AgouMNTeyo4 [58:38]).

**When to apply** — As a worked example of a prior belief tested by two designs (lab mechanics and field cohort) and reported when it failed. Also when a coaching rule rests on tradition: ask what the stress measure and the field outcome actually show.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's mission is to help the team "answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones" rather than hand down answers unilaterally (Explicit, Playbook p.6). Inference: Fleisig reversing a position his own center held is the posture that mission describes. Eric has said he does not apply constraints-led or cueing frameworks he does not fully understand (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q25), which is not specific to this topic.

**When NOT to apply** — Baseball pitching in youth to professional levels; the torque comparison does not transfer to any football skill. The speaker does not show the torque numbers for the three curveball studies or the cohort statistics, so the "same or less" result is as stated. "Not proven dangerous" is not "safe", as he says himself (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31]). The cohort is the same one that shows the 100-innings result, and the tested pitches did not include the split-finger. A rule about when to introduce a pitch is a coaching and medical decision; do not remove an age guideline on this result alone.

**Example** — The speaker's own contrast: ASMI's advice before the studies against its results (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [40:42]).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (same cohort); [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]] (the 2017 speaker on fastball usage and velocity as risk factors); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]].

---

# Defining "proper mechanics" as the mean and spread of healthy, high-velocity pitchers

**What it is** — Asked how he knows what proper mechanics are, Glenn Fleisig describes his criteria: the pitcher came to his lab, had not been injured for at least a year, and had a high fastball velocity during the test (AgouMNTeyo4 [54:32], [55:03]). He took about 150 such pitchers (Roger Clemens-level names and "some college guy you never heard of"), computed the mean and standard deviation of each measurement (stride length is his example), and calls that range proper mechanics: "the 150 best pitchers I've ever tested by ball velocity" (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33]). Studies then showed pitchers outside those ranges, as a group, had lower ball velocity and higher stress on the arm (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33], [56:03]). He has also tested over 2,000 pitchers in the lab, including eight who went on to win Cy Young awards (caption "sa young", "15 sa young Awards"), with 12 cameras and about 40 markers (AgouMNTeyo4 [13:20], [13:51], [43:13]).

His own account of the limits: when asked whether pitchers measured with poor mechanics later got hurt, "it was a mixed bag", about half did and half did not. He says mechanics is only one factor, that his lab intervenes by telling pitchers what they do wrong (so some may fix it), and that the step from higher arm stress to more injury is "a leap of faith" that he has not proven (AgouMNTeyo4 [58:06], [58:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that good mechanics give more velocity and less arm stress, and bad mechanics more stress (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45]). Inference: the benchmark is built from a selected, healthy, fast group, so a measure outside the range is a flag for a closer look, not a finding of risk.

# Spring training field lab: pitchers back from UCL surgery looked mechanically like never-injured pitchers

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig describes a study done with Major League Baseball in the 2014 spring training in Arizona and Florida, where his group brought the motion-capture lab (in a tent or outdoors) to the teams instead of bringing pitchers to Birmingham (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:16], [26:17]). Design: 40 pitchers who had had the surgery a couple of years earlier and had made it back to spring training, against 40 never-injured pitchers; each filled out a form, had range of motion measured lying on a table, then had a full kinematics and kinetics test (AgouMNTeyo4 [25:47], [26:17], [26:47]).

He named four hypotheses before looking (AgouMNTeyo4 [26:47], [27:18], [27:49], [28:21]):
- The returners show compensation, "messed up" elbow and shoulder mechanics.
- They hold back: stand more upright and push the elbow rather than driving as they did.
- The "inverted W": the arm is late and still down at foot contact, measured as arm external rotation at foot contact.
- A low elbow that is then raised, a stressful pattern.

Result: both groups threw about 85 mph in spring training and matched on height and weight; he found no difference in flexibility and no difference in mechanics (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:21], [28:52]). His reading: minor leaguers who make it back have typical flexibility and mechanics, "when it works it works" (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22]).

**Why it works** — The design works because it names each hypothesis as a measurable pattern before testing; the speaker gives no mechanism for the null result. Inference: if returners were compensating, the group means would differ on the four named patterns, and they did not.

**When to apply** — As a template for a field comparison of a return group against matched controls: define the comparison group, name hypotheses as measurable patterns in advance, and take the lab to the athletes when the athletes cannot come to the lab.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's contribution to return to performance is "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4); assessment is repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April," Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). The baseline does not document a return-group comparison at Baylor.

**When NOT to apply** — Fleisig lists the limits himself: only minor leaguers were studied, only after they made it back (no pre-injury mechanics), and only success stories, not the "10 or 20%" who did not return (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:52], [29:22], [29:53]). A null result in 40 against 40 does not exclude small differences, and the talk gives no effect sizes. At the time of the talk the study had "just got published". Baseball pitchers only; do not infer a football return standard. The group is selected on having come back healthy.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a never-injured pitcher and a returner both at about 85 mph, indistinguishable on the four patterns (AgouMNTeyo4 [28:21]).

**Related** — [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]]; [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]] (a design that would capture the pre-injury data this study lacked; Inference).

# Fatigue is individual: read it with people who know the athlete, and read it the next day

**What it is** — Asked how coaches and parents know when a pitcher has reached the fatigue level, Glenn Fleisig answers in his Q&A (AgouMNTeyo4 [49:59], [50:29]):
- His group tried to measure fatigue scientifically from muscle activity, "it doesn't work".
- Pitcher and coach cannot figure it out at the moment of the game; they need to know each other beforehand (a tough guy, recent problems, how he walks after getting hurt), and no one wants a player pitching while thinking "I think it hurts a little" (AgouMNTeyo4 [50:29]).
- What is decided is not at game time but afterward: in the training room the trainers are "a key for reading when a guy is better, when it is normal and when it's not normal". A pitcher who used to need two days of recovery and now needs three is a signal; he says pro teams will skip or bump a start on trainer feedback (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:00], [51:30]).
- The athlete's education is for the next day: pain in the elbow or shoulder is not normal; full-body fatigue is normal; feeling full-body fatigue in the game "is your body saying let's call it a day" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30], [52:01]).
- Summary line: "fatigue is individual" (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:30]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no data for this answer; it is his stated practice among the pro teams and trainers he talks to. Inference: it uses the one signal he trusts, a person who sees the athlete every day and compares to that athlete's own normal, which fits a result that fatigue behavior was the largest risk marker while no instrument measured it.

**When to apply** — When a monitoring system needs an escalation path: define who reads the athlete the next day, what counts as a change from his own normal (recovery taking longer, pain versus tiredness), and what action follows a flag.

Eric's baseline: the coach's eye flags where to look and data then investigates (interview 2026-09-28, Q6, Explicit); a trained eye is treated as at least as important as technology for daily assessment (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). Daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes gamed them, kept for return to play and chronic conditions (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and mRSI from daily CMJ testing replaced them as the readiness marker (Explicit, same source). Inference: Fleisig's answer partly conflicts with the mRSI choice, since it relies on trainer and athlete report; Eric's keeps subjective input only where context is needed, such as return to play. Recovery is managed through load design, with nothing objective tracked (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q23).

**When NOT to apply** — Assertion from one expert answer, not tested; he says himself that measurement attempts failed. It presumes trainers or coaches who see the athlete daily and a written trigger for what happens after a flag. Pitching context: one start every fifth day, with a next-day check; do not copy the "next day" timing to football's weekly cycle without Baylor's own staff routine. Self-report can be gamed (Eric's survey experience above). Fatigue and pain are not distinguished by any test in the talk.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a pitcher whose recovery moved from two days to three, which the trainer notices and which can lead the team to skip a start (AgouMNTeyo4 [51:00], [51:30]).

**Related** — [[claim--pitching-while-fatigued-is-the-largest-retrospective-odds]]; [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] (Old Bull).

# Players, parents and coaches overestimate what Tommy John surgery does

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB, director of league economics and strategy, sHXuxj3-rbQ [00:02], [00:37]) says a perception had grown that the surgery is always successful and returns a pitcher within a year throwing harder, and that players should have it before an injury to improve performance (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [05:46]). A survey designed by a Yankees physician (caption "dr. mod"; the 2015 talk's caption "Dr Ahmad ... the New York Yankees doctor", probably the same survey, unconfirmed) went to youth players, coaches and parents asking how successful the surgery is, how long it takes, and whether the player will throw harder (sHXuxj3-rbQ [05:46]). Results as the speaker reports:
- More than half of high school players thought a player should have the surgery without an actual elbow injury.
- More than half of college players thought pitch speed increases afterward (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:17]).

Fleisig's 2015 account of what appears to be the same survey gives different numbers: about two-thirds of respondents guessed about 60 percent make it back, about a third thought velocity goes up, a third to a half thought performance improves, and 25 to 50 percent thought surgery makes sense in some cases even without an injury, which he calls "frightening" (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:30], [19:01], [19:33]). He adds that pro teams sometimes tell him a hurt pitcher should "just go get a surgery and get it over with", which is "not the right attitude", and that doctors say surgery is a last resort (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:00]). The two talks give different splits by group; do not harmonize them.

The speaker's response: the third part of the Pitch Smart program (see the program entry) gives accurate information so that players see surgery as "something I want to avoid, not something I want to have" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:55]).

**Why it works** — Neither speaker gives a mechanism for why the perception formed; DeAngelo lists it as one of the league's 2014 concerns (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:10]). Inference: when a rare success story (a star pitcher returning at full velocity) is visible and the outcome distribution is not, a perception gap forms, and measuring it is the first step in correcting it.

**When to apply** — As a method: before a recovery or rehab education effort, survey the athletes, coaches and parents on what they believe about outcomes, and compare to published outcomes. Also as a caution when staff or athletes describe a procedure as performance-enhancing.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's four operating principles include Research and Development and Performance Team Collaboration (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and in return to performance it contributes "Testing and progression", with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4). The baseline holds no education survey of athletes' beliefs.

**When NOT to apply** — Baseball pitchers' beliefs about one surgery; the survey sample sizes, response rates and wording are not shown in either talk. The speaker says "all of our research and all the research of the medical community" shows the beliefs are incorrect, but Fleisig reports that one of three studies found performance improved after surgery (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:05], [21:39]), so "incorrect" on performance is contested (see the return-rate entry). The speaker is a league-office official describing the league's program. Do not use belief percentages from one talk as a Baylor estimate.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the survey result that more than half of high school players thought surgery without injury was reasonable (sHXuxj3-rbQ [05:46], [06:17]).

**Related** — [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]] (2015 talk: what the outcome studies show); [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]].

# Players, parents and coaches overestimate what Tommy John surgery does

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB, director of league economics and strategy, sHXuxj3-rbQ [00:02], [00:37]) says a perception had grown that the surgery is always successful and returns a pitcher within a year throwing harder, and that players should have it before an injury to improve performance (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [05:46]). A survey designed by a Yankees physician (caption "dr. mod"; the 2015 talk's caption "Dr Ahmad ... the New York Yankees doctor", probably the same survey, unconfirmed) went to youth players, coaches and parents asking how successful the surgery is, how long it takes, and whether the player will throw harder (sHXuxj3-rbQ [05:46]). Results as the speaker reports:
- More than half of high school players thought a player should have the surgery without an actual elbow injury.
- More than half of college players thought pitch speed increases afterward (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:17]).

Fleisig's 2015 account of what appears to be the same survey gives different numbers: about two-thirds of respondents guessed about 60 percent make it back, about a third thought velocity goes up, a third to a half thought performance improves, and 25 to 50 percent thought surgery makes sense in some cases even without an injury, which he calls "frightening" (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:30], [19:01], [19:33]). He adds that pro teams sometimes tell him a hurt pitcher should "just go get a surgery and get it over with", which is "not the right attitude", and that doctors say surgery is a last resort (AgouMNTeyo4 [18:00]). The two talks give different splits by group; do not harmonize them.

The speaker's response: the third part of the Pitch Smart program (see the program entry) gives accurate information so that players see surgery as "something I want to avoid, not something I want to have" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:55]).

The baseline holds no education survey of athletes' beliefs.

# Pitch Smart: a three-part program of count limits, plain-language research and accurate surgery information

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes how the league office turned a medical committee's research into a youth program. In 2014 the Commissioner's Office convened leading medical experts (the speaker names the orthopedist Dr Andrews and ASMI's research director, caption "dr. fly cigs", plus team physicians and researchers) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:52]). They told it that the single greatest factor was youth overuse and rest, and that "very modifiable" behaviors correlated with injury in youth; the best study followed youth pitchers for ten years and found 100 or more innings a year went with more serious arm injury (sHXuxj3-rbQ [07:22], [07:54]). GMs, coaches and players also said specializing early and playing year round with high single-game pitch counts raised risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:24]).

The program, with USA Baseball, launched in November 2014 (caption "pitch mark", "pitch smart", read here as Pitch Smart) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:54], [12:30]). Three parts (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [09:55]):
- Pitch count limits and required rest guidelines from age 7 to 22, with allowed pitches rising by age and rest days rising with pitches thrown in a game; example: throw 50 pitches, wait two days before pitching again (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [10:25]).
- Research synthesized into digestible information for players and coaches, so they understand why.
- Accurate information about Tommy John surgery.

Adoption (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:03], [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]): Little League already had guidelines; showcase circuits (caption "perfect game") and college summer leagues including the Cape Cod League comply; in 2014 Vermont was the only state with a pitch-count-based high school rule; in 2016 the National Federation of State High School Associations voted to require states to adopt a pitch-count and required-rest rule; in 2017 the speaker counts 44 or 46 states (the caption is ambiguous) with Connecticut and Massachusetts as holdouts. States do not all follow the Pitch Smart table exactly.

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that the research already existed and "the idea if you throw 50 pitches you have to wait two days" is "a pretty intuitive concept" that had not been adopted (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24]). He gives no evidence that adoption reduced injuries. Inference: the program's contribution is distribution and compliance, not new evidence, which is how an overuse rule becomes a rule.

**When to apply** — As a model for converting a research finding into an enforceable exposure rule: name an authority, set limits that scale by age and dose, publish the reasons, and recruit governing bodies. Inference: for Baylor, the equivalent is a written exposure rule a staff member can apply the same way each time.

Eric's baseline: smooth, gradual progression is treated as protective and abrupt changes as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); in-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (Inferred, transcript and shared slides, not claimed in interview). Inference: a pitch count with rest is a dose rule of that kind. The baseline holds no throwing or contact-exposure rule.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `untested` because the talk shows no outcome for the program: the speaker said surgeries leveled off and did not claim the guidelines caused it (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:37]). He works for the league office and describes the league's own program. The age and pitch table is not reproduced in the transcript, so no specific limit can be cited from this talk. Youth baseball pitchers; do not transfer to football. The 2012 concussion speaker, discussing pitch counts, calls the age caps "clearly not based on much science" (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]), a caution on how much weight a count table can bear.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 2016 high school federation vote, from one state with a rule to nearly all (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (the 2015 talk's cohort result behind the guideline); [[claim--mlb-surgery-counts-leveled-off-after-2014-with-no-causal-link]]; [[framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count]]; [[claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents]].

# MLB Tommy John surgery counts spiked in 2012 to 2014, then leveled off, but the talk does not link that to the program and also says injuries are rising

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB league office) reports the trend from the public surgery database (caption "baseball heat mass", back to 1974) and from the league's electronic medical record (required of all clubs since 2010; he says league data are not shared publicly until ready for peer review) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09], [01:39]).

The 2012 to 2014 spike (sHXuxj3-rbQ [02:41], [03:12], [03:42], [04:12]):
- Disabled list days for the elbow injury were at an all-time high from 2012 to 2014, a 72% increase over the three years before (the injury is garbled in the caption as "Elvis trees").
- MLB surgeries: the previous high was 22; 36 in 2012; 31 in 2014.
- More of the players were 25 or younger than in any earlier five-year bucket, and many were top young pitchers; recovery is 12 to 16 months.
- The number having a second surgery rose steadily from 1995 to 2014.

The leveling off (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:06], [15:37]): roughly 20 to 25 players a year still have the procedure but "we didn't see the exponential growth" feared; the number of players drafted who had already had the surgery rose steadily to 2014, then was relatively flat over the last three years, though 2016 set an all-time high. In Q&A he says the minor league record shows no linear upward trajectory, "goes up and down" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22], [25:55]).

The speaker does not claim the program caused the leveling off.

Contradiction inside the talk: in the Q&A he compares eras and says "the data kind of suggests ... that injuries are increasing" even though teams are more careful (sHXuxj3-rbQ [28:14], the captions are garbled around this sentence); that sits against the leveled-off statements at [14:36] to [15:37]. Another speaker in 2015 (Fleisig) said professional surgeries were still climbing and that youth and high school numbers had been "curbed a little" but were still going up (AgouMNTeyo4 [07:42], [47:52]).

**Why it works** — Neither speaker gives a mechanism for the trend. Inference: a short window after a spike mixes a plateau with ordinary year-to-year noise; one or two years do not make a trend, as the speaker says himself in the Q&A ("tough to judge one or two-year trends", sHXuxj3-rbQ [25:22]).

**When to apply** — When a policy is credited for a leveling off in an injury count: check the window length, the denominator and whether the same data also say the opposite.

Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19), and no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a count of cases without exposure (innings, pitches, athletes at risk) cannot support a causal story about a program.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `contested` because the talk both says the count leveled off and says injuries are increasing, and the 2015 talk describes a still-rising trend; the dates differ, so these may be consistent, but the 2017 Q&A is unclear. The leveling off rests on 2 to 3 years after a spike. There is no exposure denominator or comparison group, and 2016 itself was a record in the draftee count. The speaker works for the league office. Baseball only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: draftees with prior surgery rising to 2014 and then flat, with a 2016 record (sHXuxj3-rbQ [15:06], [15:37]).

**Related** — [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]]; [[claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree]] (2015 prevalence and return data); [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]].

# Rest alone for partial UCL tears: 93% of 43 players returned without surgery, and tear location may predict who fails

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes two team-physician studies of the league's own players, in the area of conservative care and rehab where he sees "very promising studies" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:42], [18:13]):
- The Colorado Rockies' study of players with partial UCL tears, in the middle ground between a full tear that means surgery and an injury that might not need it: after six to eight weeks of rest, 93% came back and pitched without surgery (caption: "pitched with that name surgery", read as without surgery). The sample was 43 players, and the speaker says "it's tough to really draw too many conclusions from that" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [18:13], [18:43]). 93% of 43 is about 40 players (Inference, my arithmetic).
- A similar study by a Cleveland Indians physician (name garbled in the captions) asked whether the location of the tear predicts who returns: players with distal tears were "much more likely to fail the rehab" and need surgery than players with proximal tears (sHXuxj3-rbQ [18:43], [19:14]).

# New recovery and training methods spread faster than the evidence for them

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) says "research sometimes lags behind what the medical community moves toward", and gives three examples (sHXuxj3-rbQ [19:44], [20:14]):
- Orthobiologics (PRP, stem cells): increasingly popular, but there have not been many peer-reviewed articles showing they work better than rest and rehab alone (sHXuxj3-rbQ [20:14]). One Los Angeles surgeon (caption "dr. Yoon") reports anecdotally better results with stem cells than PRP; another (caption "dr. Ella trash", likely ElAttrache) makes the same confounding point: patients wait three, four, six or eight weeks, so "is it the rest or is it the ortho biologic?" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [20:44], [21:16]). Of the MLB pitchers who used them in 2016 (from the public database): one came back successfully (caption name "Michael Lorenzen"), three had already had surgery, and four were still waiting (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:16], [21:47]).
- Club technology and training methods: clubs want an edge and use devices to track fatigue, injury risk and stress variables; a Seattle outfit (caption "drivelines") with "unorthodox training methods" has become popular among some teams, and "it's tough to tell whether this actually helps" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [22:18], [22:49], [23:19]). A team that succeeds in one area is copied by others (sHXuxj3-rbQ [23:19]).
- A repair technique: Dr Dugas (caption "dugas @andrew sports medicine") repairs the UCL with tape augmentation, with an expected recovery of about six months instead of 12 to 16 (the caption reads "six to six months post 12 to 16", garbled); experimental, for certain tears only, with early positive results in high school and college players and two Cardinals pitchers expected back for spring training (sHXuxj3-rbQ [23:52], [24:22]). The speaker says the medical community approaches it "with skepticism" awaiting research.

His summary: "there's still a lot to learn", and it is "difficult to make any sweeping statements based on the data that we have" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:47]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is competitive pressure and imitation (sHXuxj3-rbQ [22:18], [23:19]). Inference: when each recovery involves a waiting period, any treatment applied at the start of the wait is confounded with rest unless a comparison arm exists.

**When to apply** — Before adopting a new recovery, rehab or monitoring technology: ask for a comparison against rest or the current protocol, and for what happens to everyone who tried it, not the successes.

Eric's baseline: a test or technology that does not answer a question someone has "doesn't have a place" (interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit); NordBord testing was retired for roster-wide use because it could not be run consistently, and kept only for small groups with a clear clinical purpose and dedicated oversight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-20); data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Recovery at Baylor is managed through load design with nothing objective tracked (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q23). Inference: the standard Eric applies to testing technology is the one DeAngelo suggests applying to recovery technology.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the speaker's claim is a general observation with a handful of examples (eight pitchers, two surgeons' opinions) and no systematic review. He is a league-office official, not a clinician, and says the surgeons' opinions are anecdote. It is not evidence that the methods do not work; the point is that the evidence is not there yet. Do not use it to dismiss a technology without a trial of your own.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 2016 list of MLB pitchers who used PRP or stem cells (one successful, three had surgery, four waiting) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [21:16], [21:47]).

# A prospective cohort: baseline tests at entry, then follow every athlete through the medical record

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes the league's most significant research project with the players association: when a player is drafted he is asked for a baseline set (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:08]):
- A shoulder and elbow MRI.
- A full biomechanical evaluation.
- A playing-history questionnaire.

Each player is then followed for the rest of his career for performance, usage and future injuries, to see whether any baseline test or later behavior predicts injury, which can then inform preventive programs (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39]). The design depends on the league's electronic medical record: since 2010 all clubs must use it, so "we don't need to continually go back to these players and ask them", which "eliminates any participation or dropout rate" (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09], [16:39]). So far 225 players are enrolled, with about 400 expected when baseline collection finishes (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11]). The research partners are the players association, club medical staff and an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins; data are not shared publicly until ready for peer review (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09]).

The committee's research questions that this study serves (sHXuxj3-rbQ [10:25], [11:26], [11:57], [12:30]): at the professional level, whether biomechanics, usage or velocity matter as risk factors; whether the rehab process or future usage can reduce second surgeries; whether surgical variants (graft, technique) affect success; and whether alternative therapies can shorten the 12 to 16 month rehab or avoid surgery.

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is that the record removes loss to follow-up, one of the main weaknesses of long cohort studies (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39]). Inference: baseline data recorded before any injury is what lets a later injury be compared to something measured earlier; the 2015 spring-training study could not do this because it met pitchers only after they had returned (AgouMNTeyo4 [29:22]).

**When to apply** — When deciding what to record at entry for each athlete so that later injuries can be studied: a short history of prior workload and injury, the physical baselines already collected, and a way to link them to later records.

Eric's baseline: each source system holds its own data and the source wins over the aggregating platform (Kitman) when they disagree (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q11); there is no common testing cadence across sports (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q9); no formal injury-risk model is in use (Explicit, Q12). Data collection is judged on cost against insight (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-19). Inference: a Baylor version would be a small intake record linked to existing VALD and GPS data, not an MRI program, and its value depends on the consistency of collection that Eric's NordBord decision stressed.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the talk reports design and enrollment only, with no results. The data are not public, so the claims cannot be checked. It rests on a league-wide record system that every club must use (sHXuxj3-rbQ [01:09]); Baylor's follow-up would depend on its own record system and on a stable staff. Teams also guard training data as a competitive advantage, so the league works with a select group of teams on granular training data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [28:44]). Professional draftees, not college athletes. The speaker works for the league office. Do not add collection until a question exists.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 225-player enrollment, with "no dropout" because follow-up is by the medical record (sHXuxj3-rbQ [16:39], [17:11]).

**Related** — [[case-study--spring-training-field-lab-post-surgery-vs-never-injured]] (2015 talk: a post-hoc comparison with no pre-injury data); [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]]; [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]].

# Throwing harder both raises injury risk and improves performance, so the goal is balance

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) answers a Q&A question on velocity: "a lot of the evidence suggests that throwing harder increases risk of injury", and there is "also a lot of evidence" that throwing harder improves performance, so a player is more likely to reach higher levels (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]). It is "tough to tell someone not to throw as hard", he says, because velocity may be essential to performing. His position: do not focus on throwing hard "to the exclusion of" mechanics and locating the ball; find a balance among them (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23], [30:53]). He also says three recent studies pointed to greater fastball usage, throwing harder, pitching more in individual games and resting less as associated with UCL injury risk, and calls the field "very preliminary" and dependent on public data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11], [17:42]). In the same Q&A he says throwing is a stressful task and injuries can be reduced but "never" eradicated (sHXuxj3-rbQ [29:22], [29:52]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and cites neither the evidence on risk nor the evidence on performance. Fleisig's 2015 talk offers a related point: poor mechanics raise arm stress and cost velocity, and good mechanics give more velocity and less stress, though the step from arm stress to injury is unproven (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45], [58:38]). Inference: if both hold, mechanics is the lever that can improve the trade, which is what "balance" asks for.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's development plan treats a single outcome number (velocity, jump height, top speed) as the target: ask what else rises with it, and track the cost alongside the gain.

Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, density and training means, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). Speed is described as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: the two baseline positions meet in this entry's tension, and the baseline does not say how Baylor resolves it for football.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an expert's general statement in a Q&A; neither the injury evidence nor the performance evidence is named, and the three risk-factor studies are "very preliminary" by his own description. It is pitching velocity in baseball, from a league-office official. Do not use it to justify limiting any athlete's speed or velocity development, or to infer a football speed-injury relationship. The 2015 speaker (Fleisig) says average fastball velocity rose by about 2 mph since 2002, from a news clip shown in his talk, not from his data (AgouMNTeyo4 [10:15]).

**Example** — The speaker's own framing: the player who throws harder is likelier to reach higher levels yet may carry more injury risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]).

**Related** — [[claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs]] (2015 talk: pitch type and elbow torque); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]].

# Throwing harder both raises injury risk and improves performance, so the goal is balance

**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) answers a Q&A question on velocity: "a lot of the evidence suggests that throwing harder increases risk of injury", and there is "also a lot of evidence" that throwing harder improves performance, so a player is more likely to reach higher levels (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]). It is "tough to tell someone not to throw as hard", he says, because velocity may be essential to performing. His position: do not focus on throwing hard "to the exclusion of" mechanics and locating the ball; find a balance among them (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23], [30:53]). He also says three recent studies pointed to greater fastball usage, throwing harder, pitching more in individual games and resting less as associated with UCL injury risk, and calls the field "very preliminary" and dependent on public data (sHXuxj3-rbQ [17:11], [17:42]). In the same Q&A he says throwing is a stressful task and injuries can be reduced but "never" eradicated (sHXuxj3-rbQ [29:22], [29:52]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and cites neither the evidence on risk nor the evidence on performance. Fleisig's 2015 talk offers a related point: poor mechanics raise arm stress and cost velocity, and good mechanics give more velocity and less stress, though the step from arm stress to injury is unproven (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45], [58:38]). Inference: if both hold, mechanics is the lever that can improve the trade, which is what "balance" asks for.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's development plan treats a single outcome number (velocity, jump height, top speed) as the target: ask what else rises with it, and track the cost alongside the gain.

Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, density and training means, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position). Speed is described as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: the two baseline positions meet in this entry's tension, and the baseline does not say how Baylor resolves it for football.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an expert's general statement in a Q&A; neither the injury evidence nor the performance evidence is named, and the three risk-factor studies are "very preliminary" by his own description. It is pitching velocity in baseball, from a league-office official. Do not use it to justify limiting any athlete's speed or velocity development, or to infer a football speed-injury relationship. The 2015 speaker (Fleisig) says average fastball velocity rose by about 2 mph since 2002, from a news clip shown in his talk, not from his data (AgouMNTeyo4 [10:15]).

**Example** — The speaker's own framing: the player who throws harder is likelier to reach higher levels yet may carry more injury risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [30:23]).

**Related** — [[claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs]] (2015 talk: pitch type and elbow torque); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]]; [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]].
